Who Has the Power? · Topic 1

The Election Nobody Understands

OVERVIEW

Find out what is on the 2026 ballot, compare the House and Senate, and explain how Congress can change while the president stays in office.

STEP 1: Open

Open Topic 1 on BeCurrent

Everything happens on the website. There is nothing to download.

STEP 2: Investigate

Use the assigned clip windows and prepared evidence cards. Complete the five-item practice and correct your choices. Submit a short source note, an application note, and a final explanation. A factual bullet, two short application bullets, and two or three final sentences are enough.

  1. Name one verified fact about the 2026 election and one outcome still unknown. Name your source.
  2. For the Indiana race card, name the office voters choose and one decision its winner could influence. Name one part of government this race does not replace.
  3. If the president is not on the ballot, why can the midterms still change who has power? Use one verified fact.

Start here frames, read-aloud support, voice typing, and agreed paper accommodations are available. Background dropdowns and Push further are optional. Political preferences are not scored.

STEP 3: Submit

Choose Gather All My Work. Paste into this Canvas Text Entry and submit. If copying is blocked, use the manual-copy box. Saving a draft on BeCurrent is not submission.

Aim to submit before lunch. Due: the start of class on Thursday, October 22.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  1. I can identify congressional offices on the ballot and explain that the presidency is not being elected.
  2. I can sort at least four of five House/Senate facts correctly and correct my errors.
  3. I can use one verified fact to explain a possible governing consequence.

SCORING: 5 points
  • What voters choose: Correctly identify Congress as the House and Senate, distinguish their election cycles, and explain that the presidency is not being elected.
  • Fact and source: Name a relevant source, accurately use a fact it establishes, and identify something it cannot establish yet.
  • Power and limit: Connect a changed majority to leadership, priorities, or oversight and explain one change it does not automatically cause.
  • Explain your thinking: Make the connection understandable in concise writing, dictated text, or the agreed paper response. Spelling and length do not determine this score.

After lunch: CNN10 and daily reporting through The Desk.

Who Has the Power? · Topic 2

The Battle for Congress

OVERVIEW

Follow individual seats to chamber control. Test how a small shift can change leaders, committees, and the agenda without guaranteeing a new law.

STEP 1: Open

Open Topic 2 on BeCurrent

Everything happens on the website. There is nothing to download.

STEP 2: Investigate

Use the assigned clip windows and prepared evidence cards. Complete the five-item practice and correct your choices. Submit a short source note, a committee lookup, an application note, and a final explanation. A factual bullet, three facts from house.gov with one or two sentences, two short application bullets, and two or three final sentences are enough.

  1. Name two decisions a new majority could influence. Identify your video or official source.
  2. Committee lookup: Which House committee did you choose? Name one subject this committee covers, from its own website. Who chairs this committee, and which party is the chair in? Then: Committee chairs come from the House majority. If a different party won the House majority in November, what could change about your committee, and what could it still not guarantee?
  3. In the 217-to-218 scenario, what could change and why is the promised law not guaranteed?
  4. Connect one district race to seats, a majority, and congressional priorities. Include one limit on that power.

Start here frames, read-aloud support, voice typing, and agreed paper accommodations are available. Background dropdowns and Push further are optional. Political preferences are not scored.

STEP 3: Submit

Choose Gather All My Work. Paste into this Canvas Text Entry and submit. If copying is blocked, use the manual-copy box. Saving a draft on BeCurrent is not submission.

Aim to submit before lunch. Due: the start of class on Monday, October 26.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  1. I can identify the majority in a constructed 435-seat House scenario.
  2. I can identify two decisions a new majority could influence.
  3. I can explain one reason chamber control does not guarantee a policy change.

SCORING: 5 points
  • Seats and majority: Use the constructed 435-filled-seat model to explain why 218 is a majority. Do not present it as an actual 2026 result.
  • Relevant evidence: Name a clip or official reference and accurately explain evidence about leaders or committees. Record one real House committee, a subject it covers, and its chair’s party from house.gov.
  • Influence and limits: Explain two decisions a majority can influence and why the other chamber or presidential action still matters for a law.
  • Explain your thinking: Make the seat-to-power connection understandable. Concise notes, dictated text, and agreed paper work can show the same learning.

After lunch: CNN10 and daily reporting through The Desk.

Who Has the Power? · Topic 3

The Power to Stop a President

OVERVIEW

Work independently through two opening clips, short notes, and a school-lunch bill lab. Answer eight worksheet questions along the way to explain congressional checks, accountability, and delay.

STEP 1: Open

Open Topic 3 on BeCurrent

Everything happens on the website. There is nothing to download.

STEP 2: Investigate

Use the assigned clip windows and prepared evidence cards. Complete the five-item practice and correct your choices. Work independently. Watch the two opening clips with headphones and read the six notes boxes on the page; no copied notes or teacher presentation is required. Answer worksheet Questions 1–8 where they appear. Questions 6–8 are the source note, application note, and final explanation, not extra tasks. Short phrases and bullets are welcome.

  1. Choose one opening clip. Name the outlet and one way a changed Congress could affect a president.
  2. Complete the idea: divided government means different parties control the presidency and ____.
  3. Does a congressional investigation prove wrongdoing by itself? Explain what oversight is meant to do.
  4. Which chamber confirms many presidential nominees: the House, the Senate, or both?
  5. Test the bill lab twice. Record one setup that blocks the bill and one that makes it law. If you use the paper route, trace the two setups from the notes.
  6. Explain two congressional checks on the president. Identify your source.
  7. Why can’t the House alone make the school-lunch proposal law? Give one benefit of scrutiny and one possible cost of delay.
  8. Can divided government improve accountability and make governing harder at the same time? Use one institutional example.

Start here frames, read-aloud support, voice typing, and agreed paper accommodations are available. Background dropdowns and Push further are optional. Political preferences are not scored.

STEP 3: Submit

Choose Gather All My Work. Paste into this Canvas Text Entry and submit. If copying is blocked, use the manual-copy box. Saving a draft on BeCurrent is not submission.

Aim to submit before lunch. Due: the start of class on Wednesday, October 28.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  1. I can accurately explain two congressional checks.
  2. I can explain why one chamber cannot ordinarily enact a law alone.
  3. I can support an accountability benefit and a governing difficulty with a specific example.

SCORING: 5 points
  • Checks and institutions: Accurately explain two congressional checks and distinguish a Senate-only confirmation power from powers both chambers exercise.
  • Relevant evidence: Name a relevant clip or official source and accurately use an institutional fact from it.
  • Accountability and governing: Use the scenario to explain both an accountability benefit and a governing difficulty, with a concrete mechanism and a limit.
  • Explain your thinking: Make the reasoning understandable without requiring a long response, public speech, or agreement with a political position.

After lunch: CNN10 and daily reporting through The Desk.

Who Has the Power? · Topic 4

The Fight for Your Vote

OVERVIEW

Watch real 2026 campaign ads, spot one-sided messaging, and verify the claims using independent records.

STEP 1: Open

Open Topic 4 on BeCurrent

Everything happens on the website. There is nothing to download.

STEP 2: Investigate

Use the assigned clip windows and prepared evidence cards. Complete the five-item practice and correct your choices. Work independently. Watch the two opening clips with headphones and read the six notes boxes on the page; no copied notes or teacher presentation is required. Answer worksheet Questions 1–8 where they appear. Questions 6–8 are the source note, application note, and final explanation, not extra tasks. Short phrases and bullets are welcome.

  1. What is the purpose of a political campaign ad? Name one way an ad tries to shape what voters notice.
  2. From the intro videos, name one technique campaigns use to persuade voters.
  3. Why is a campaign website or ad not enough to prove a factual claim?
  4. BEFORE CHECKING: What does Ad A want viewers to believe? What does Ad B want viewers to believe?
  5. Choose one ad. What audience, image, word, or emotion does it use to persuade?
  6. Choose one checkable claim from either ad. What independent record could help test it?
  7. AFTER CHECKING: What did the independent evidence establish, and what important context was left out of the campaign ads?
  8. Why does a favorable poll not prove a candidate won, and why does a campaign promise not guarantee a new law?
  9. AFTER CHECKING: What did the independent evidence establish, and what important context was left out of the campaign ads?
  10. Choose one checkable claim from either ad. What independent record could help test it?
  11. Why does a favorable poll not prove a candidate won, and why does a campaign promise not guarantee a new law?

  2. I can name a second source and explain what it supports, contradicts, or leaves unresolved.
  3. I can explain why a poll or promise does not establish what will happen.

SCORING: 5 points

  • Ad analysis: Identify both ads' messages, a persuasive choice, and a checkable claim.
  • Evidence and revision: Name a relevant independent source, identify a limit or omitted context, and update the first impression.
  • Poll and promise limits: Distinguish sampled opinion and proposed policy from verified outcomes.

Who Has the Power? · Midterms 5

Reading a Real Ballot

OVERVIEW

Read the real sample ballot for one Zionsville precinct, find the facts printed on it, think about what it asks voters to decide, and plan how you would check a question before voting. Then gather your answers into Canvas.

STEP 1: Open

Open Reading a Real Ballot on BeCurrent

The real Eagle 01 sample ballot is on the page, all 8 pages. Everything happens on the website. There is nothing to download.

STEP 2: Answer

Work down the page on your own. 22 short questions in 4 parts:

  1. Part 1: Ballot scavenger hunt (12 questions). Every answer is printed somewhere on the ballot. A word or short phrase is enough.
  2. Part 2: Think about it (4 questions). Answer in one or two sentences.
  3. Part 3: Before you decide (4 questions). A voter only sees a few lines of text on the ballot. Good voters find out more before they vote. Choose one public question and answer about it.
  4. Exit question (2 questions). Last one. Then gather your work.

A word or short phrase is enough for Part 1. One or two sentences is enough everywhere else. Sentence starters, read-aloud support, voice typing, and agreed paper accommodations are available.

STEP 3: Submit

Choose Gather All My Work. Paste into this Canvas Text Entry and submit. If copying is blocked, use the manual-copy box. Saving a draft on BeCurrent is not submission.

Aim to submit before you leave today. Due: the start of class on Thursday, November 5.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  1. I can find the offices, candidates, and public questions printed on a real ballot.
  2. I can explain why a ballot is mostly local and state offices, and why that matters.
  3. I can name what I would need to know before voting on a public question, and a trustworthy place to find it.

SCORING: 5 points
  • Finds the facts: Part 1 answers match what is printed on the ballot.
  • Explains the ballot: Part 2 answers give a reason tied to the ballot, not a party preference.
  • Plans a check: Part 3 names real questions and a trustworthy source for one public question.

Your answers are private. You never have to say how you or your family would vote, and nobody is asked to share with the class. Political preferences are not scored.

Who Has the Power? · Midterms 6

Election Results: What Happened and Why?

OVERVIEW

Watch CNN 10 and three reports on Tuesday night’s results, read what a survey of voters says about why Democrats won, then look up who won on Zionsville’s own ballot. Gather your answers into Canvas.

STEP 1: Open

Open Election Results: What Happened and Why? on BeCurrent

The videos, the article and the result links are all on the page. Everything happens on the website. There is nothing to download.

STEP 2: Answer

Watch the videos together, read the article, then work down the page on your own. 16 questions in 3 parts:

  1. Part 1: Why did Democrats win? (7 questions). Use the article above. Answer in one or two sentences, in your own words. Each question tells you which section to look in.
  2. Part 2: A warning for the winners (3 questions). Use Section 5 of the article. One or two sentences each.
  3. Part 3: What happened here at home? (6 questions). On Tuesday you read the real ballot for one Zionsville precinct. Now find out how those races turned out. Use the result links below and write the source for each answer. A short phrase is enough.

One or two sentences is enough for Parts 1 and 2. A short phrase and a source is enough for most of Part 3. Sentence starters, read-aloud support, voice typing, and agreed paper accommodations are available.

STEP 3: Submit

Choose Gather All My Work. Paste into this Canvas Text Entry and submit. If copying is blocked, use the manual-copy box. Saving a draft on BeCurrent is not submission.

Aim to submit before lunch. Due: the start of class on Monday, November 9.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  1. I can answer questions about the article using its numbers and examples in my own words.
  2. I can explain why something happened in the election, not just what happened.
  3. I can name the winner of a Boone County or Indiana race and the source where I found it.

SCORING: 5 points
  • Uses the article: Parts 1 and 2 use the article’s numbers and examples, in your own words.
  • Explains why: Answers give a reason (because, so, which led to), not only a fact.
  • Finds the results: Part 3 names the results and the source for each one, and keeps unofficial results labeled as unofficial.

Your answers are private. You never have to say how you or your family voted, and nobody is asked to share with the class. Political opinions are not scored; using the evidence is.

After lunch: daily reporting through The Desk.
